books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142

stimulus.text:
“That all political disabilities imposed by the third section of the fourteenth article of amendments of the Constitution of the United States are hereby removed from all persons whomsoever, except Senators and Representatives of the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh Congresses, officers in the judicial, military, and naval service of the United States, heads of departments, and foreign ministers of the United States.”

—Amnesty Act, May 22, 1872 (17 Stat. 142)
stimulus.source_note: Amnesty Act of May 22, 1872, ch. 193, 17 Stat. 142. Public domain (federal statute; text verified against the Statutes at Large as quoted by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and Congress.gov).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Amnesty Act’s main effect was to

options.text: pardon Confederate soldiers for all crimes committed during the war.
options.misconception: The Act removed political disabilities, the bar on holding office, not criminal punishment.

options.text: give freedpeople the right to vote in Southern elections.
options.misconception: Background: Black voting rights came from the Fifteenth Amendment, not from the Amnesty Act.

options.text: let most former Confederates hold public office again.
remove federal troops from the Southern states.
options.misconception: Background: troops stayed until 1877; the Act said nothing about the Army.

rationales.A: The Act removed political disabilities, the bar on holding office, not criminal punishment.
rationales.B: Background: Black voting rights came from the Fifteenth Amendment, not from the Amnesty Act.
rationales.C: The Fourteenth Amendment had barred former Confederates who broke their oaths from holding office. The Act lifted that bar for nearly everyone, so the men who had led the rebellion could run the South’s governments again.
rationales.D: Background: troops stayed until 1877; the Act said nothing about the Army.
rationales.general:
1. The Act’s key words are “political disabilities,” the penalty the Fourteenth Amendment laid on oath-breakers.
2. It removes those disabilities from “all persons whomsoever,” with only a few high officials excepted.
3. That means the men who led the rebellion could hold office again.
4. The exception list is small, so the restoration was nearly complete.
Remember: removing a penalty is a policy choice, and this one chose to welcome the old leadership back.
